task.goal: Explore why a clap seems quieter at different positions in an empty hallway without installing equipment or exposing anyone to loud sound.
hard_constraints: A group has one afternoon, a phone sound meter used only for aggregate level, and a tape measure.
No recordings of voices, hazardous volume or blocking the hallway.
Consider distance, reflections and background noise; no claim of calibrated acoustics.
task.available_resources: Several safe standing points and a quiet baseline period.
task.expected_result: Distinct explanations and an observable comparison.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Distance reduces the direct sound
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether increasing source-to-listener distance explains the quieter clap. Sound spreads as it travels, so its direct contribution generally decreases with distance. Hallway reflections can weaken or disrupt that trend; do not assume a precise inverse-square relationship.

Choose three safe standing points along a clear section of hallway, measured from one fixed clapping position. Use the same person making comfortable, gentle claps, with unchanged hand position and direction. Move the phone and one listener between the marked distances, keeping microphone height and orientation consistent. Nobody stands in a doorway or obstructs passing traffic. The phone displays aggregate levels only, with audio recording disabled.

This requires sufficiently similar background conditions and reasonably repeatable claps. Phone processing and reflected sound may obscure small differences, so readings establish only relative patterns, not calibrated acoustics.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Measure a quiet baseline at each point. At each distance, use an equal-duration measurement window containing the same number of spaced, gentle claps. Repeat the sequence in reverse order to check for drift. Record the displayed aggregate level and the listener’s simple quieter/similar/louder judgment. Compare the nearest and farthest points first. Consistently lower readings and quieter judgments farther away support distance as a contributor. Similar or reversed results weaken a distance-only explanation and suggest reflections, background changes, or measurement limitations. If clap windows cannot be distinguished from baseline, treat the phone comparison as inconclusive rather than clapping louder.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reflections change sound at equal distances
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether hallway boundaries redistribute the audible sound independently of distance. Walls, corners and open doorways can return or redirect sound, changing the combination of direct and reflected energy reaching a listener. Positions at the same source distance can therefore sound different. The exact pattern depends on geometry and surface materials and cannot be predicted confidently from appearance alone.

Keep the clapper fixed and use the tape measure to identify two accessible listening points at approximately equal distances: for example, one near a side wall and another nearer the hallway centre. Choose locations that remain clear of traffic, and maintain the same phone height and orientation relative to the source. Use gentle, repeatable claps and aggregate-only phone measurements with recording disabled.

The prerequisites are a usable equal-distance pair and similar background levels. This comparison cannot isolate individual echoes, reverberation time or frequency effects. Differences in the clapper’s radiation direction and phone response remain possible confounders.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First inspect the layout and measure baseline aggregate levels at both points. Alternate between the points using identical measurement-window durations and equal numbers of gentle claps. Ask the same listener whether either position sounds quieter or more lingering. Repeat with the clapper facing a different direction while preserving the geometry. The simple comparator is the expectation that equal-distance points would behave similarly if distance dominated. A repeatable difference that survives the orientation change supports a boundary-related explanation; a difference that reverses with orientation implicates source direction instead. No consistent difference weakens this explanation for the selected pair, without ruling out reflection effects elsewhere.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Background noise masks an otherwise similar clap
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether a clap seems quieter because it stands out less against the background. Ventilation, distant movement or other ordinary hallway noise can reduce a clap’s perceptual prominence even when the clap itself has not become weaker. A noisier location may consequently produce a higher total phone reading while making the clap harder to notice.

Hold source and listener positions fixed and compare the supplied quiet baseline period with a naturally occurring, modestly noisier period. Do not create extra noise, solicit voices or increase clap strength. Use the same gentle clapper, distance, orientation and phone placement throughout. Disable audio recording and retain only displayed aggregate levels and written judgments.

This requires background conditions to vary naturally within the afternoon. If they do not, the comparison remains untested. Aggregate readings cannot separate clap energy from background energy or establish a perceptual masking threshold. Any conclusion is therefore about a plausible contribution, not a calibrated signal-to-noise measurement.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During each condition, measure a background-only window, followed by an equal-duration window containing the same number of spaced, gentle claps. Have the listener judge how clearly the claps stand out. Repeat a quiet condition afterward if possible, giving a quiet–noisier–quiet comparison that checks for changing clap technique or listener expectations. Do not subtract decibel readings as though they were linear sound energy. Support for masking would be reduced clap prominence during the higher-background condition, with prominence returning when quiet returns, despite unchanged geometry. The simple comparator is the quiet condition. Similar prominence across conditions weakens masking as the main explanation; inconsistent claps or changing traffic make the result inconclusive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Head orientation changes how much sound reaches each ear
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A clap may seem quieter at one position because the listener turns their head differently there. The head and outer ears filter incoming sound according to its direction; the head can particularly reduce higher-frequency sound reaching the farther ear. This can change a clap’s apparent sharpness and loudness even without changing source distance. The effect may be modest in a reflective hallway, where sound arrives from several directions.

Use one gentle clapper, one listener, the tape measure and the phone displaying aggregate levels only, with recording disabled. Select two safe standing points where the difference was noticed, measure their distances from the fixed clapper, and note the listener’s usual facing direction at each. At each point, compare facing the clapper with turning sideways while keeping the listener’s location fixed. Keep the clapper’s position and orientation unchanged. Place the phone consistently at each point and leave it stationary during head turns.

This assumes the listener can comfortably change orientation and the claps are reasonably repeatable. It requires no installed equipment or additional sound source. Distance remains a possible explanation between points, reflections may dilute directional hearing, and background noise may alter judgments. The phone cannot measure what reaches either ear or establish calibrated acoustic levels.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Measure a short background-only baseline at each point. Give the listener the same small number of spaced, comfortable claps facing forward and sideways, then repeat in reverse order. Ask only for quieter, similar or louder judgments. Pause for passersby or changing noise; never increase clap strength to obtain a reading.

The simplest comparator is the same location with a different head orientation. A repeatable judgment change during head turns, while aggregate phone readings remain broadly similar, supports an orientation contribution. Then compare both positions while facing the clapper at each: a reduced positional difference adds support. If orientation produces no repeatable change and the original positional difference persists, this explanation is weakened. Variable claps or background make the result inconclusive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Changing clap strength creates an apparent position effect
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Separate a location effect from changes in how the clap is produced. Hand alignment, cupping and effort change the sound emitted by a clap. If listeners visit positions in a fixed sequence while the clapper gradually becomes gentler, later positions can seem quieter even when position is not the main cause.

Use one fixed clapper and two safe listening points, with distances measured by tape. Keep the clapper’s posture and facing direction consistent and use only comfortable, gentle claps. The phone displays aggregate levels without recording audio. No equipment is installed, and everyone pauses or steps aside for traffic.

The distinguishing mechanism is variation at the source. Distance and reflections can still create real differences between listening points; background noise can obscure either effect. This approach requires enough repeatability to compare short blocks, but does not assume that individual claps are identical. Phone readings are relative observations, not calibrated measurements or proof of equal source output.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First leave the phone and listener at one reference point. Measure background, then compare several equal-duration blocks containing the same number of gentle claps. Variation at unchanged geometry demonstrates how much apparent change the source and measurement process can produce.

Next compare listening points A and B in an A–B–B–A order, moving the phone with the listener and preserving its height and orientation. Use the same measurement windows and clap counts, and note quieter/similar/louder judgments. Measure background at both points and repeat once if time permits.

The simple comparator is the variation observed at the fixed reference point. If the apparent difference follows trial order or is comparable to ordinary fixed-position variation, source inconsistency remains a plausible explanation. A repeatable A-versus-B difference across reversed order weakens a source-variation-only account. Aggregate readings cannot establish which individual clap changed; indistinguishable readings remain inconclusive, without increasing volume.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Visual expectations alter the loudness judgment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether seeing the hallway and the clapper contributes to the impression of quietness. Perceived loudness depends partly on attention and expectations: a visibly distant source or a spacious-looking location may influence judgments alongside the sound reaching the ears. Removing visual information briefly can test for a visual contribution without altering hallway acoustics.

Use a fixed gentle clapper and one stationary listener at each of two safe standing points. Measure source distances and keep the listener facing the source with the same head orientation. Compare listening with eyes open and comfortably closed. Closing eyes is optional and happens only while standing still, clear of traffic, with another participant watching the surroundings. The phone remains stationary during each comparison and displays aggregate levels only; audio recording stays disabled.

This requires a willing listener and reasonably stable background conditions. Closing the eyes also changes attention, so any effect supports a visual or attentional contribution rather than proving a particular expectation. Distance and reflections remain physical explanations, and background noise may change prominence independently.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Measure a background-only baseline at each point. At the first point, present equal small groups of spaced, gentle claps with eyes open, closed, closed and open. Keep source technique, phone placement and measurement duration consistent. Ask for quieter/similar/louder judgments between adjacent groups without suggesting an expected direction. Reverse the starting eye condition at the second point.

The simplest comparator is eyes open versus closed at the same location, where distance and boundary geometry remain unchanged. Then compare the listener’s positional judgments under each eye condition. A repeatable reduction in the positional difference with eyes closed, alongside broadly similar phone readings within each location, supports a perceptual contribution.

If the positional difference persists equally under both conditions, this explanation is weakened. Changes in phone readings, background noise or head position make the comparison ambiguous. The listener still knows their approximate location, so a null result cannot exclude every expectation effect; no calibrated acoustic conclusion follows.

EXPAND.title: The clapper sends different amounts of sound in different directions
EXPAND.proposal:
A clap need not radiate equally in every direction. Hand shape and orientation can change the sound sent toward a listener, so positions at similar distances may receive different direct sound. This is a source-direction explanation, although reflections can modify the observed pattern.

Use one fixed clapping point and one fixed listening point, measured with the tape. Keep the phone beside the listener at constant height and orientation. The same person makes gentle claps with a consistent hand shape, first with their hands oriented one way and then turned approximately a quarter-turn. Keep the hand contact point as stationary as practicable. Nothing needs to be installed, and everyone must remain clear of traffic. Use only displayed aggregate levels, with recording disabled.

The necessary assumption is that the clapper can change orientation without substantially changing clap strength. Establishing that perfectly is beyond these resources. A consistent orientation effect would make source direction a plausible contributor to differences between hallway positions; it would not establish a radiation pattern or calibrated acoustic measurement.
EXPAND.experiment: Measure a quiet background window, then alternate the two hand orientations over four equal-duration windows containing the same small number of spaced, gentle claps. Compare aggregate readings and the listener’s quieter/similar/louder judgments. Fixed distance is the simple comparator; alternating order reduces drift. Repeat at a second safe listening position if time allows. An orientation effect that changes with listening direction supports this explanation. No repeatable effect weakens it for these claps. Changing background, inconsistent hand contact or strong reflections can make the result inconclusive. Do not increase volume if the phone cannot distinguish clap windows from baseline.

EXPAND.title: The listener’s head and ears change the received sound
EXPAND.proposal:
A listener’s orientation can affect a clap’s apparent loudness and clarity. The head partially shields an ear, especially at higher frequencies, and the outer ears respond differently to sounds arriving from different directions. If people naturally face different ways at different hallway positions, some apparent position dependence could come from the listener.

Keep the clapper, listener and phone at fixed measured positions. The listener turns in place between facing the clapper and facing sideways, without moving closer or farther away. Keep the phone stationary and pointed consistently; it serves as a rough check on changing source or background conditions, not as a model of human hearing. Use comfortable, gentle claps, aggregate measurements only, and no audio recording.

This needs a safe place to turn without obstructing traffic and a listener comfortable doing so. Effects may be subtle, individual and dependent on the clap’s frequency content. Reflections arriving from many directions may reduce orientation differences. A change in perceived sharpness alone should be reported as such rather than automatically called a loudness change.
EXPAND.experiment: Take a quiet baseline, then compare facing-forward and sideways listening in alternating order, using equal windows and equal numbers of gentle claps. Ask separately whether each set seems quieter and whether it seems less sharp. Repeat with the opposite side facing the source. The comparator is unchanged geometry with only listener orientation varied. Repeated perceptual changes alongside broadly similar phone readings support a receiving-orientation contribution, though aggregate readings cannot prove identical claps. No consistent perceptual change weakens the explanation. To connect the finding to the original observation, revisit two hallway positions while maintaining the same facing direction relative to the source; a persistent position difference needs another explanation.

EXPAND.title: The claps themselves vary between position trials
EXPAND.proposal:
The apparent hallway effect may partly originate in the source: ordinary hand claps vary in strength, contact shape and duration. If someone unconsciously claps more softly during a particular position trial, the position receives credit for a change that began at the hands. This is variation between sound events, distinct from sound spreading or being redirected after emission.

Use two safe listening points at measured distances from a fixed clapper. Place the phone at a separate, fixed reference point near enough to obtain useful relative readings from gentle claps, while keeping everyone comfortable and the walkway open. Leave the phone’s height and orientation unchanged. One listener alternates between the two positions while the clapper maintains the same stance and hand orientation. Record only aggregate displays and written judgments.

The phone is an imperfect source reference: its reading includes background and reflections, and its processing may conceal differences. Nevertheless, with the phone, source and surroundings stationary, substantial changes between repeated windows flag instability in the stimulus. This explanation is most useful for checking whether an apparent position effect survives reasonably comparable claps.
EXPAND.experiment: Measure background at the phone reference point and inspect background conditions at both listening points before returning the phone to its fixed reference. Run four brief sets in an A–B–B–A listening order, each with the same number of gentle claps and the same measurement duration. Record the phone’s aggregate level and the listener’s judgment for each set. Compare variation between repeated visits to the same point with variation between points. If quieter judgments coincide with lower reference readings regardless of position, source variation is plausible. If the reference remains broadly stable and the position difference repeats, source variation becomes a weaker explanation; distance, reflections or local background remain candidates. If gentle claps are indistinguishable from baseline, this check is inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Comparison order and loudness memory can create an apparent position effect
EXPAND.proposal:
A clap’s judged loudness can depend on the preceding listening experience. People retain an imperfect memory of loudness, and repeated similar sounds can become less noticeable as attention wanes. If the group always visits positions in the same order, a later position might seem quieter partly because of that order. This is a perceptual comparison mechanism: it need not produce a corresponding reduction in the phone’s aggregate reading.

Use two safe standing points, A and B, measured from one fixed clapper. Keep the clapper’s stance and hand direction consistent and use only gentle, comfortable claps. One listener visits both points, while the phone remains at a fixed reference location with consistent height and orientation. Record written loudness judgments and displayed aggregate levels only; disable audio recording. Nobody closes their eyes while walking or obstructs the hallway.

The comparison requires reasonably repeatable claps, enough time to reverse the visiting order, and background conditions that remain broadly similar. Distance and reflections can cause genuine differences between A and B, while background noise can alter prominence. Order effects could coexist with those mechanisms. Phone readings provide a rough check for changing conditions, not calibrated measurements or proof that successive claps were identical.
EXPAND.experiment:
First inspect the quiet background at A and B using equal-duration aggregate readings. Then conduct four short paired visits in the order AB, BA, BA, AB, allowing the same brief settling interval at each stop. At each point give the same small number of gently spaced claps; after each pair, the listener writes which location seemed louder, or “no clear difference,” without consulting earlier judgments.

The simple comparator is a stable position effect: A or B consistently sounds quieter regardless of visiting order. An order contribution is supported if the second-visited point repeatedly seems quieter even when the positions reverse. If the same physical point remains quieter across both orders, the proposed order explanation is weakened. Inconsistent judgments are inconclusive; this small exercise cannot distinguish memory, attention and ordinary trial variability.
